articles.title: Self-Hosted Agent Observability: What to Evaluate Before Deploying
articles.excerpt: A good self-hosted observability tool for AI agents is Langfuse, Opik or Arize Phoenix if you want software you run yourself for free; Agnost AI self-hosts only as an Enterprise VPC deployment and is…
articles.body: A good self-hosted observability tool for AI agents is Langfuse, Opik or Arize Phoenix if you want software you run yourself for free; Agnost AI self-hosts only as an Enterprise VPC deployment and is not open source. Agnost AI is the pick if you need conversation-level failure detection, alerts and fix PRs on top of traces inside your own cloud, with audit logs and custom SLAs under an Enterprise contract. For open source, Langfuse (MIT except its ee folders) and Opik (Apache-2.0) are the most complete; Phoenix is free to self-host with no feature limits but is source-available under the Elastic License 2.0.
articles.author: Shubham Palriwala

articles.title: What I Learned from Building and Testing a Task Management REST API
articles.excerpt: Building a backend project is not just about making APIs work. It is also about checking whether they behave correctly in different situations. During my internship at Valentius Kryptix, I worked on a…
articles.body: Building a backend project is not just about making APIs work. It is also about checking whether they behave correctly in different situations. During my internship at Valentius Kryptix, I worked on a Task Management REST API project that helped me understand this in a practical way. The project was built using Node.js, Express.js, and MongoDB. Its main purpose was to allow users to register, log in, and manage their personal tasks through API endpoints. Understanding the Backend Functionality The API supports basic task management operations such as creating, viewing, updating, and deleting tasks. It also includes task statuses like pending, in-progress, and completed. One important part of the project was user authentication.

articles.title: Best Braintrust alternatives for evaluating AI agents (2026)
articles.excerpt: The best Braintrust alternatives for evaluating AI agents are Agnost AI for evaluating agents in production, LangSmith for LangChain and LangGraph teams, and Langfuse or Opik for open-source evals you…
articles.body: The best Braintrust alternatives for evaluating AI agents are Agnost AI for evaluating agents in production, LangSmith for LangChain and LangGraph teams, and Langfuse or Opik for open-source evals you can self-host for free. Agnost AI runs online evals on every real production conversation, alerts you when they fail, and opens fix pull requests tested against past runs; it does not replace Braintrust's offline datasets or experiments, so pair it with one of the offline tools. For that offline half: Arize gives you a free self-hosted workbench (Phoenix) with a managed upgrade (AX), Confident AI with DeepEval or Promptfoo run evals as tests in CI, and Splunk Agent Observability (formerly Galileo) or W&B Weave fit teams already on those platforms.
articles.author: Shubham Palriwala

articles.title: Your CI Pipeline Wasn't Built for Agents
articles.excerpt: Every CI pipeline I've ever tuned had a person on the other end of it. Someone pushed a few times a day, went for coffee while the build ran and came back to read the failure. The runner pool, the tim…
articles.body: Every CI pipeline I've ever tuned had a person on the other end of it. Someone pushed a few times a day, went for coffee while the build ran and came back to read the failure. The runner pool, the timeouts and the order of the jobs all assumed that rhythm without anyone writing it down. Coding agents don't keep that rhythm. One opens a pull request, pushes a fix, pushes a fix to the fix and opens three more PRs before lunch. Every push starts the same workflow you sized for a team of humans. So the pipeline turns into the slow part of the loop. Then somebody asks you to make it faster. In a regulated shop, that request is where the danger starts. Look at the queue first Before you touch a single test, pull the step timings from your recent runs. Use the median and ignore the worst run.

articles.title: LangSmith vs Langfuse vs Braintrust vs Arize (2026): which to use for a production agent, and what else to consider
articles.excerpt: To monitor a production agent, use LangSmith if you build on LangChain or LangGraph, Langfuse if you need open source and free self-hosting, Braintrust if your releases run on experiments and scored d…
articles.body: To monitor a production agent, use LangSmith if you build on LangChain or LangGraph, Langfuse if you need open source and free self-hosting, Braintrust if your releases run on experiments and scored datasets, and Arize if you want Phoenix free on your own infrastructure or AX's managed session-level evals; and yes, consider Agnost AI if the failures you care about only show up across whole production conversations. Agnost AI judges every production conversation against plain-language rules, with no sampling, and turns failures into tested pull requests, but it has no offline datasets, experiments or CI gating, so it usually runs next to one of the four rather than replacing it.

articles.body: One of Grand Theft Auto 6 ’s strangest random encounters occurs when you’re offering taxi services, and a man with a beard wearing a dark suit and sunglasses climbs into the backseat with a gun. This can happen if you’re playing as either Jason or Lucia, but both scenes play out the same way: The man wants you to run a red light, ignore phone calls, and drive him to Harborside Park in Vice Beach. He also sounds an awful lot like Tom Cruise, with a calm but forceful demeanor that seems almost sociopathic . articles.body: Sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics .
